summary.title: Major concerns with the integrity of the mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier in dodecyl-phosphocholine used for solution NMR studies
summary.authors: Martin S King; Paul G Crichton; Jonathan J Ruprecht; Edmund R S Kunji
summary.executive_summary: This paper presents a critical analysis of a previous study by Brüschweiler et al. that claimed to refold the yeast mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier (AAC3) from inclusion bodies using the detergent dodecyl-phosphocholine (DPC) for solution NMR studies. The authors argue that DPC is too harsh for AAC3, leading to immediate loss of tertiary structure and inactivation. They present evidence from isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC), NMR, and thermostability assays demonstrating that the binding affinities reported for the DPC-refolded protein are orders of magnitude weaker than those observed for native, membrane-embedded AAC3. Specifically, the Kd for carboxyatractyloside (CATR) binding to DPC-refolded AAC3 was reported as ~150 µM, whereas the authors' measurements on native AAC3 show a Kd of ~72 nM, a difference of 200 to 2000-fold. Furthermore, functional reconstitution assays showed that AAC3 diluted into DPC prior to reconstitution lost its ability to transport ADP, whereas control samples in mild detergent retained activity. The authors conclude that the DPC-refolded protein is in a non-native, unfolded state, rendering the NMR data biologically irrelevant. They highlight that the high positive charge of AAC3 and the negative charge of ligands at neutral pH may lead to non-specific interactions in the DPC environment, further complicating the interpretation of the previous NMR results. The paper underscores the importance of using mild detergents like dodecyl-maltoside for studying membrane proteins to preserve their native structure and function.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper presents a critical analysis of a previous study by Brüschweiler et al. that claimed to refold the yeast mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier (AAC3) from inclusion bodies using the detergent dodecyl-phosphocholine (DPC) for solution NMR studies. The authors argue that DPC is too harsh for AAC3, leading to immediate loss of tertiary structure and inactivation. They present evidence from isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC), NMR, and thermostability assays demonstrating that the binding affinities reported for the DPC-refolded protein are orders of magnitude weaker than those observed for native, membrane-embedded AAC3. Specifically, the Kd for carboxyatractyloside (CATR) binding to DPC-refolded AAC3 was reported as ~150 µM, whereas the authors' measurements on native AAC3 show a Kd of ~72 nM, a difference of 200 to 2000-fold. Furthermore, functional reconstitution assays showed that AAC3 diluted into DPC prior to reconstitution lost its ability to transport ADP, whereas control samples in mild detergent retained activity. The authors conclude that the DPC-refolded protein is in a non-native, unfolded state, rendering the NMR data biologically irrelevant. They highlight that the high positive charge of AAC3 and the negative charge of ligands at neutral pH may lead to non-specific interactions in the DPC environment, further complicating the interpretation of the previous NMR results. The paper underscores the importance of using mild detergents like dodecyl-maltoside for studying membrane proteins to preserve their native structure and function.

Research Context
The subject is the yeast mitochondrial ADP/ATP carrier AAC3. The authors have previously solved its structure by electron and x-ray crystallography. They have studied its interactions with specific inhibitors atractyloside and carboxyatractyloside. The critique targets a claim that AAC3 can be refolded from inclusion bodies. The refolding was claimed to use the detergent dodecyl-phosphocholine (DPC). The authors claim AAC3 is maintained in a folded and active state. This state was claimed to persist during ITC and NMR experiments. The authors argue that DPC leads to immediate loss of tertiary structure. DPC causes inactivation of AAC3 when isolated from the inner membrane. AAC3 was folded and active in the mitochondrial inner membrane. This activity was shown by functional complementation. The authors question the validity of the refolded protein's integrity. They note that no other functional assays were performed. Specifically, transport assays were not done to verify activity. The authors highlight a discrepancy in reported binding affinities. Published Kd values for CATR binding are in the low nanomolar range. This is consistent with the role of CATR as a powerful toxin. The authors' own measurements show ADP transport is half-maximally inhibited by 1.2 nM CATR. This consensus is at least three to four orders of magnitude lower. The Kd values reported for refolded AAC3 in DPC are much higher.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether AAC3 refolded in DPC retains its native structure. The hypothesis is that DPC causes immediate loss of tertiary structure. The authors predict that DPC-refolded AAC3 will be inactive. They hypothesize that the binding affinities in DPC will be significantly weaker. The authors expect the Kd for CATR binding to be in the nanomolar range. They predict that functional transport assays will fail for DPC-refolded protein. The authors question whether the observed NMR signals are specific. They hypothesize that the perturbations may be non-specific interactions. The authors predict that thermostability assays will show a non-native state in DPC. They expect that CATR will not stabilize the protein in DPC. The authors hypothesize that the DPC-refolded protein is unfolded. They predict that the protein will not form proteoliposomes with activity. The authors question the validity of the dynamic studies by NMR. They hypothesize that CATR binding should lock the protein in a non-dynamic state. The authors predict that the observed dynamics do not provide a plausible mechanism.

Methodological Details
The study used yeast mitochondrial AAC3 purified from inner membranes. The protein was purified in dodecyl-maltoside/tetraoleoyl cardiolipin. Isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC) was used to measure CATR binding. The ITC experiments were conducted at 10 °C. Carboxyatractyloside was titrated into purified 25 μM AAC3. The titrant was 500 μM CATR in buffer. Injections were 2 μL at 3-min intervals. Thermostability assays used the fluorophore CPM. The temperature was increased from 25 to 90 °C. Protein unfolding was monitored by fluorescence emission. CATR:AAC3 molar ratios ranged from 0 to 100. The protein concentration was approximately 1 μM. Reconstitution assays used L-α-phosphatidylcholine and tetraoleoyl cardiolipin. The lipid was mixed in a 20:1 (w/w) ratio. Proteoliposomes were formed by removing detergent with Bio-Beads. ADP uptake assays used radiolabeled [14C]-ADP. The final working concentration was 1.5 µM [14C]-ADP. Uptake was measured at various time points up to 15 min. The assays were performed on a Hamilton MicroLab Star robot. The filter plates had a pore size of 0.45 µm.

Procedures And Architectures
AAC3 was purified using a Ni-Sepharose high performance column. The column was washed with 40 column volumes of buffer. The buffer contained 20 mM PIPES pH 7.0 and 150 mM NaCl. The protein was cleaved with Factor Xa overnight at 10 °C. The cleaved protein was separated by filtration and centrifugation. The protein was snap-frozen and stored in liquid nitrogen. For thermostability, CPM was diluted 50-fold into buffer. Approximately 1.5 μg of purified protein was added. The final volume was 45 μL. Fluorescence was measured on a Qiagen Rotorgene Q. Excitation light was at 440--480 nm. Emission was detected at 505--515 nm. Measurements were made in 1 °C intervals. The ramp rate was 5.6 °C/min. For ITC, samples were degassed under vacuum for 20 min. The stirrer speed was 350 rpm. For reconstitution, lipid was dried under a nitrogen stream. The lipid was emulsified with pentaethylene glycol monodecyl detergent. 30 μg of purified AAC3 protein was added. Detergent was removed using Bio-Beads SM-2. The proteoliposomes were exchanged into external buffer. The suspension was diluted 9-fold before ADP uptake assays.

Key Results
The Kd for CATR binding to DPC-refolded AAC3 was reported as ~150 µM. The authors' ITC measurements on native AAC3 gave an average Kd of 72 nM. This is 200 to 2000-fold lower than the reported values. The Kd for ATR binding was corrected to 192 nM in an erratum. The Kd for ADP binding by NMR was 500 μM. This is ~85-fold higher than published consensus values. Thermostability assays showed a typical melt curve in dodecyl-maltoside. In DPC, a high signal was observed with no transition. CATR addition had no effect on stability in DPC. Dilution into DPC resulted in complete loss of CATR-sensitive ADP uptake. Control tests in dodecyl-maltoside retained activity. The chemical shift perturbations for CATR binding were dynamic. These residues are not near the known CATR binding site. The Kd of CATR binding to folded AAC3 is in the low nanomolar range. The enthalpic change is low and the apo-state is unstable.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The data suggest that DPC-refolded AAC3 is in a non-native state. The high affinity of CATR for native AAC3 is due to polar interactions. These interactions cross-link the transmembrane α-helices. The ring of transmembrane α-helices is held by lateral pressure. Unliganded AAC3 in detergent micelles is prone to unfolding. The extremely low affinity in DPC questions the specificity of binding. The dynamic nature of the perturbations is inconsistent with tight binding. The high positive charge of AAC3 may promote non-specific interactions. The observed dynamics do not provide a plausible mechanism for transport. The results have no biological relevance.

Contradictions And Limitations
The authors note that the ITC experiments were very difficult. Only 2 out of 10 trials succeeded. The enthalpic change is low and the apo-state is unstable. There are very few polar side chain interactions in AAC3. The authors question the validity of the dynamic studies. The observed dynamics do not provide a plausible mechanism. The authors note that the Kd values in DPC are much higher. The authors argue that the DPC-refolded protein is inactive. The authors highlight the lack of functional assays in the original study. The authors note that the NMR signals may be non-specific.

Claims
DPC-refolded AAC3 is in a non-native, unfolded state. Thermostability assays showed no transition in DPC. CATR addition had no effect on stability in DPC. Dilution into DPC resulted in complete loss of ADP uptake. The original study claimed AAC3 was folded and active in DPC. The NMR data from DPC-refolded AAC3 are biologically irrelevant.
The binding affinities reported for DPC-refolded AAC3 are significantly weaker than for native AAC3. The Kd for CATR binding to native AAC3 is 72 nM. The Kd for CATR binding to DPC-refolded AAC3 is ~150 µM. This is a 200 to 2000-fold difference. The original study reported a Kd of ~15 µM by ITC. The DPC-refolded protein does not retain its native binding properties.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The authors performed thermostability assays to assess protein stability. They used CPM to monitor unfolding. They compared stability in dodecyl-maltoside and DPC. They performed reconstitution assays to test functional activity. They measured ADP uptake in proteoliposomes.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1a shows ADP transport inhibition by CATR. Figure 1b shows ITC measurements of CATR binding. Figure 1c shows thermostability in dodecyl-maltoside. Figure 1d shows thermostability in DPC. Supplementary Table 1 lists Kd values for CATR binding. Supplementary Table 2 lists Kd values for ADP binding. Supplementary Fig. 1a shows the ring of transmembrane α-helices. Supplementary Fig. 1b shows CATR binding interactions. Supplementary Fig. 2 shows ADP uptake assays.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the demonstration that DPC-refolded AAC3 is non-native. 2. The strongest evidence is the 200 to 2000-fold difference in Kd values. 3. The future path is to use mild detergents for studying membrane proteins.
